intuition.summary: Fractions f/g with g(a) != 0 in a coordinate ring are functions that make sense on some neighbourhood of the point a; the localization R_P is the ring of such 'local functions', which is where the name comes from. Localizing at a different point kills everything supported at a point (zero ring).
intuition.source: Gathmann, Commutative Algebra notes, Ch.6 Motivation and Example 6.25

intuition.summary: Picture a/s, with s nonvanishing on a subspace Y, as a germ of a function near Y; the notes recommend keeping this picture in mind while working with the algebra.
intuition.source: Math 210B (Stanford, Winter 2008) localization handout, §1 (author not given in the extracted text; likely B. Conrad's course)

intuition.summary: Germs of smooth functions at a point of a manifold form a local ring: a germ is invertible exactly when it does not vanish at the point, so the vanishing germs are the unique maximal ideal and evaluation identifies the residue field with R.
intuition.source: J. Armstrong, The Unapologetic Mathematician, 'Local Rings' (2011)

intuition.summary: Localizing at a prime 'zooms in' to germs at a point, but Zariski open sets are dense, so Zariski-local isomorphism is still quite global (it forces birational equivalence); completion is the finer, formal neighbourhood in which regular points of equal dimension look alike.
intuition.source: C. Grossack, 'Why is the completion of a local ring more local than just localizing?' (blog, 2022)

intuition.summary: Localization keeps the information near a point and discards non-local information; localizing Z at powers of 10 gives decimal fractions, a concrete picture of 'allowing chosen denominators'.

Under the duality between rings and spaces, inverting S corresponds to restricting to the complement of the locus where elements of S vanish; Spec R[S^{-1}] -> Spec R are the basic open immersions of the Zariski topology.
intuition.source: nLab, localization of a commutative ring (Idea; geometric interpretation)

motivation.summary: Chevalley (1944) explains that for a coordinate ring o of a variety V and prime u, o/u describes the subvariety U while the ring of quotients o_u is the tool for studying a neighbourhood of U in V; local theory needs non-domains because completion creates zero divisors, which forced a general construction.
motivation.source: C. Chevalley, 'On the notion of the ring of quotients of a prime ideal', Bull. AMS 50 (1944) 93-97

motivation.summary: History: Grell introduced localization for integral domains; Chevalley and Uzkov generalized it; Krull's 1938 paper launched local rings and their dimension theory (regular local rings = nonsingular points); Cohen's 1946 structure theory of complete local rings followed.
Krull introduced local rings in 1938 as 'Stellenringe' (rings of a point); the English term 'local ring' is attributed to Zariski.
Algebraic motivation: make chosen elements invertible, as Q extends Z, so that questions about rings and modules reduce to a union of smaller local problems.

In number theory localization lets one work in local rings (DVRs such as Z_(p)) where ideals are simple, and recover global information because an ideal of a domain is the intersection of its localizations; Dedekind domains are defined by their localizations being DVRs.
Localization at elements R[1/f] is the ring-theoretic input for affine schemes and the structure sheaf (O(D(f)) = R_f, stalks R_p).

definitions.summary: Construction: on A x S set (x,s) ~ (y,t) iff (xt - ys)u = 0 for some u in S; classes x/s with the usual fraction operations. The extra u is needed for transitivity when S has zero divisors.

Universal property: A -> S^{-1}A sends S to units and every ring map inverting S factors uniquely through it (Prop 10.9.3); this pins S^{-1}A down up to unique isomorphism, which is why the construction can be replaced by any model.
definitions.source: Stacks Project Prop. 10.9.3; Vakil §2.3.1 (calls the universal-property definition 'cleaner')

definitions.summary: Module localization S^{-1}M defined by the same fraction construction; it is isomorphic to M ⊗_A S^{-1}A, and is a left adjoint (Altman-Kleiman make universal properties primary and derive the tensor description from adjointness).
definitions.source: Gathmann Lemma 6.19; Vakil Ex. 2.3.K, 2.5.G; Altman-Kleiman Preface; Sutherland §2.3

definitions.summary: S^{-1}M is the filtered colimit of the M_f over f in S; localization at a single element uses S = {1,f,f^2,...}.
S^{-1}R-modules are the same as R-modules on which every s in S acts bijectively (localization is reflection onto this subcategory).
For a domain, S^{-1}A can be defined as a subring of Frac(A): A ⊆ S^{-1}A ⊆ Frac A. Agreement with the general construction is immediate because the u-factor is unnecessary without zero divisors.
R_f ≅ R[x]/(fx - 1) (adjoin an inverse); proof by checking both satisfy the universal property. Used constructively (Rabinowitsch trick).
definitions.source: standard; memory (Lombardi 2308.09371 §3 refers to Rabinowitsch's trick)

definitions.summary: Saturation: S and its saturation (all divisors of elements of S) give the same localization; two multiplicative sets give isomorphic localizations iff they have the same saturation. Saturated multiplicative sets that are maximal correspond to complements of primes.
definitions.source: Wikipedia Localization; Stanford 210B notes §8; Lombardi Fait 1.20

definitions.summary: Local ring equivalent definitions: unique maximal ideal; non-units form an ideal; 1 != 0 and for each x, x or 1-x is a unit; a unit finite sum has a unit term. Equivalence: non-units lie in maximal ideals, so a unique maximal ideal is exactly the set of non-units.

Chevalley's 1944 ring of quotients: first divide o by the intersection Σ of primary ideals missing S, then take ordinary fractions; for Noetherian o this agrees with the modern S^{-1}o (kernel of o -> S^{-1}o is that intersection of primary components) [agreement statement from memory].
Local homomorphism: f:(R,m)->(S,n) with f(m) ⊆ n, equivalently f^{-1}(n) = m, equivalently f reflects units.

viewpoints.summary: Geometric: R_P = functions regular near a point / subvariety; R_f = functions on the open set D(f); Spec S^{-1}R is the subspace of primes missing S.

Categorical: localization is the left adjoint/reflection to the inclusion of S-inverting algebras (or modules where S acts invertibly); module localization = base change ⊗ S^{-1}A; filtered colimit of R_f.

Homotopical: the same universal property defines localization of E∞-rings; nLab treats localization away from an ideal as a modality in arithmetic cohesion and notes the clash with 'localization of a category'.
viewpoints.source: nLab, localization of a commutative ring (E∞ section)

viewpoints.summary: Constructive: instead of localizing at all primes (needs choice), use finitely many comaximal elements s_i and the rings A[1/s_i]; 'dynamical' local rings treat primes as latent objects so abstract local-global proofs become algorithms.

Formalization: a proof assistant cannot treat R[1/f][1/g] and R[1/fg] as equal, only uniquely isomorphic; one must choose a convenient characterizing property (Mathlib uses predicates like IsLocalization alongside the construction Localization).
viewpoints.source: K. Buzzard, 'Grothendieck's use of equality' arXiv:2405.10387 (via HackerNoon repost); Guan-Hu 2510.24818

viewpoints.summary: Analytic: germs of continuous/smooth/analytic functions at a point form local rings; this is the model for O_{X,x}.
viewpoints.source: Armstrong blog; Wikipedia Local ring examples

viewpoints.summary: Number-theoretic: Z_(p) is a DVR with residue field F_p and p-adic valuation; Dedekind = Noetherian domain whose localizations at nonzero primes are DVRs.

Computational: in a localization at a point one computes with local monomial orders and Mora's tangent-cone algorithm, or by computing over the polynomial ring and localizing at the end (pruning complexes), since R_p is not finitely generated over R.
Noncommutative: localization exists for any set but is well behaved under the Ore condition; key example rings of differential operators (microlocalization).

conventions.summary: Notation: S^{-1}A (Stacks, Atiyah-Macdonald, Gathmann), R[S^{-1}] (nLab), A_S (Lombardi); A_p or A_(p) for prime complement (Stanford 210B writes A_(P)); A_f vs A[1/f]; Coykendall-Kettinger (2510.10018) write the localization at {±α^n} as D[1/α].
conventions.source: Stacks 10.9; nLab; Lombardi §1.3; Stanford 210B notes; Coykendall-Kettinger §4

conventions.summary: 'At' vs 'away from': algebraists localize 'at a prime p' (Z_(p), invert everything outside (p)) but 'away from p' when inverting p (Z[1/p]); category theorists 'localize at' the morphisms being inverted, which clashes; nLab switched some pages to 'away from' and the nForum thread ended without consensus.
Older usage (before ~1960, e.g. Chevalley's standing hypothesis, and the Nagata/French tradition) required local rings to be Noetherian, calling the general case 'quasi-local'; modern texts do not.
Whether the zero ring is local: standard definition (unique maximal ideal) excludes it; Lombardi's constructive definition ('non-units form an ideal'-style axiom) counts the trivial ring as local.
Construction-first (Atiyah-Macdonald, Gathmann, Stacks, Sutherland) vs universal-property-first (Vakil 'cleaner', Altman-Kleiman throughout).
Writing '=' for canonical isomorphisms of localizations (EGA 'identifier canoniquement', Milne's stated convention) vs strict equality in proof assistants.

Equivalence relation written with different letters/orders: (xt - ys)u = 0 (Stacks), u(as' - a's) = 0 (Gathmann), (a's'' - a''s')t = 0 (Stanford 210B), u(ta - sb) = 0 (Sutherland, Xu). Same condition.
Notation (R, m, k) for a local ring with maximal ideal m and residue field k is standard in the commutative-algebra literature (e.g. Koszul survey uses 'local ring R with residue field k').

examples.summary: Z localized: at Z\{0} gives Q; at powers of p gives Z[1/p]; at the prime (p) gives Z_(p) = fractions with denominator prime to p (a DVR, residue field F_p); at powers of 10 gives decimals.
Field of fractions (S = nonzero elements of a domain) and total ring of fractions (S = non-zero-divisors).
Zero ring: S^{-1}A = 0 iff 0 ∈ S; in particular A_f = 0 when f is nilpotent (D(f) empty).

Line pair V(xy) ⊂ A^2: near (1,0) the function y equals 0, and indeed y/1 = 0/1 in the localization because x·y = 0 with x a unit there — the canonical illustration of the u-factor and non-injectivity.
Local rings: fields, DVRs, k[[x]], k[x]/(x^n) (dual numbers), Z_(2) (odd denominators), germs of functions, kG for p-group G in char p. Non-examples: k[x], Z, Z/(pq).
Local ring of A^n at a point: {g/h : h(o) != 0}; intersection multiplicity of two plane curves at o as dim_k O_o/(f,g), e.g. tangential cusps computed in OSCAR.

Not every property is local: being an integral domain is not (e.g. Z/6 or k×k: all localizations at primes are fields but the ring is not a domain) [specific example from memory]; Wikipedia notes an infinite product of fields as a cautionary example for local-global behaviour.
UFD need not be Dedekind (k[x,y]) and Dedekind need not be UFD (Z[√-13]); every PID is Dedekind because its localizations at nonzero primes are DVRs.
Spec Z_(p) has exactly two points, (0) and (p): primes of Z contained in (p). Generally Spec A_p = primes contained in p.
examples.source: Gathmann Cor 6.10 (general statement); two-point example from memory

computation.summary: Prime ideals of S^{-1}A ↔ primes of A disjoint from S (via extension/contraction); primes of A_p ↔ primes contained in p, so A_p is local with maximal ideal pA_p. Every ideal of S^{-1}A is extended.
computation.source: Gathmann Prop 6.7, Cor 6.10; Stacks Lemma 10.9.16; Sutherland Thm 2.1

computation.summary: I^{ec} = {b : sb ∈ I for some s ∈ S} and J^{ce} = J; I^e proper iff I ∩ S = ∅; primary decompositions localize by dropping components that meet S.

Exactness: S^{-1} is exact (S^{-1}A is flat), so it commutes with kernels, cokernels, quotients, finite sums, intersections, radicals: S^{-1}(M/N) = S^{-1}M/S^{-1}N; S^{-1}A/S^{-1}I = (image of S)^{-1}(A/I).
Localization in stages: (SS')^{-1}A ≅ S̄^{-1}(S'^{-1}A); e.g. (A_f)_g = A_{fg}, and localizing R_p further at a smaller prime.

Local-global: M = 0 iff M_m = 0 for all maximal m; exactness, injectivity, ideal containment, reducedness, length, projectivity/projective dimension, global dimension, Cohen-Macaulayness, regularity are checked locally.
computation.source: Gathmann Prop 6.27, Cor 6.26; Guan-Hu 2510.24818 Lemmas 2.9, 2.14, 4.12, Thm 5.20

computation.summary: Hom commutes with localization for finitely presented M: S^{-1}Hom_A(M,N) ≅ Hom_{S^{-1}A}(S^{-1}M,S^{-1}N).

Computer algebra: Macaulay2 lacks monomial orders for general R_p; at maximal ideals use Mora's tangent cone algorithm (local orderings 1 > x_i); otherwise compute over the polynomial ring, prune, and localize. OSCAR provides localization(R, complement_of_point_ideal(...)) and vector_space_dimension for multiplicities.
Comaximal covers: to check a property of A, find s_1,...,s_m generating the unit ideal and check over each A[1/s_i]; finitely presented/projective modules become free on such a cover.

confusions.summary: Why the extra factor u (or t) in the equivalence relation: without it transitivity fails when S has zero divisors; for domains it can be dropped.
A -> S^{-1}A need not be injective; injective iff S contains no zero divisors.
An element a/b of A_p can have a representation with b ∈ p; membership in A_p is about the existence of some representation with denominator outside p.

General localizations S^{-1}R are not local rings; only localization at a prime (complement of a prime) is guaranteed to be local. Also 'localization at a prime' inverts the complement, not the prime.
confusions.source: Gathmann (pitfalls); Chevalley 1944 notes that inverting only non-zero-divisors need not be local

confusions.summary: Notation clash Z_p: localization at p (or at powers of p, depending on author) vs p-adic integers vs Z/pZ; Z_(p), Z[1/p], completion Ẑ_p and Z/p are different objects.
confusions.source: Gathmann (pitfalls, Ex 6.6); D. Zack Garza notes 'disambiguating completion and localization'

confusions.summary: Ideal correspondence: every ideal of S^{-1}A is extended, but contraction-extension is a bijection only on primes (and primaries) disjoint from S, not all ideals.
Not every property is local (integral domain is not); local-global works for properties stable under the relevant intersections/exactness.
Localization vs completion: R_p already is 'germs at p' but is still Zariski-coarse; completion is 'more local'.
Are R[1/f] and R[1/g] equal when D(f) = D(g)? Only canonically isomorphic; careless identification is an issue in formalization.
Terminology 'at' vs 'away from' and 'localization of a category' meaning something different.
